replacement: Ivan left Alyosha and walked home to Fyodor Pavlovitch’s house. But oddly, a crushing gloom settled on him, and it grew heavier with every step he took toward the house. Being gloomy was nothing odd. What was odd was that Ivan could not say why. He had often been low before. And it was hardly surprising that he felt low now, when he had cut every tie that had brought him here and was about to start afresh, that very day, on a new and unknown future. He would be as lonely as ever. He had great hopes, and great—too great—expectations of life, but he could not have said clearly what his hopes were, or his expectations, or even what he wanted.
“Substantially nothing—just for the sake of conversation.”
“They’ll think I’m an accomplice, because I told him the signals as a great secret.”
“Blast it! What makes you so certain you’re going to have a fit, confound you? Are you laughing at me?”
“Confound it! If you’re laid up, Grigory will be keeping watch. Tell Grigory ahead of time, and he’ll certainly keep him out.”

“And why would he go to father at all, least of all sneaking in, if Agrafena Alexandrovna isn’t coming, as you say yourself?” Ivan went on, going white with anger. “You say so yourself, and the whole time I’ve been here I’ve been sure it was all the old man’s notion and that the creature won’t come to him. Why would Dmitri burst in on him if she doesn’t come? Speak up, I want to know what you’re thinking!”

“Nonsense!” cried Ivan, nearly beside himself. “Dmitri won’t come to steal money and kill my father to get it. He might have killed him yesterday over Grushenka, the frantic, savage fool, but he won’t steal.”
